title: A Daily Cup of Dahi and a 30-Minute Walk May Slow Aging at the Cellular Level, Study Finds
excerpt: A clinical trial published in Aging showed that yogurt, moderate exercise, and dietary tweaks reduced the pace of biological aging by 2.2% in just 12 weeks — independent of weight loss.
body:
If your nani ever told you that a bowl of dahi a day keeps the doctor away, science is finally catching up.

A clinical trial published in the journal *Aging* found that consuming 100 grams of plain yogurt daily, combined with 30 minutes of walking three days a week and basic dietary adjustments, slowed the pace of biological aging by approximately 2.2 percent over just 12 weeks. The reduction was measured at the DNA level using DunedinPACE, a tool that calculates how quickly the body is aging based on epigenetic markers — and it happened independently of weight loss.

## What the Researchers Did

The trial, conducted in Japan, enrolled 48 overweight men between the ages of 50 and 74. Half followed a structured wellness routine: daily probiotic yogurt, individualized dietary counseling that emphasized cutting sugary drinks and avoiding overeating, and walking or using a stepper machine for roughly 30 minutes at least three days a week. The other half maintained their usual habits.

Blood samples taken before and after the 12-week intervention revealed that the intervention group experienced a statistically significant slowdown in their pace of biological aging. The researchers also observed improvements in a DNA marker linked to kidney function.



> **"Blood samples taken before and after the 12-week intervention revealed that the intervention group experienced a statistically significant slowdown in their pace of biological aging."**


Remarkably, the 2.2 percent reduction in aging pace was comparable to what a previous two-year U.S. study achieved through a much more demanding 25 percent caloric restriction diet — suggesting that modest, sustainable lifestyle changes may pack a disproportionate punch.

## Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For South Asian families, the findings carry a particular resonance. Dahi — plain, unsweetened yogurt — is already a daily staple across Indian households, served with rice, used in raita, or eaten as chaas (buttermilk). The probiotic properties of homemade dahi have been celebrated in Ayurvedic tradition for centuries, long before the Western gut-health movement adopted fermented foods.

But the study's real power lies in its simplicity. It did not require gym memberships, meal-replacement shakes, or expensive supplements. A cup of yogurt, a short walk, and cutting back on snacks — habits that are accessible whether you live in Mumbai, Mississauga, or Mountain View.

South Asians face disproportionately high rates of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic syndrome, often developing these conditions a decade earlier than other populations. A growing body of research, including the MASALA study from Northwestern, has shown that this elevated risk persists even among those who report healthier diets and lower alcohol consumption — a paradox that makes preventive lifestyle interventions all the more urgent.

## The Caveats

The study's limitations are significant: it involved only 48 men of a single nationality over three months. The researchers acknowledged that larger, longer, and more diverse trials are needed to confirm whether these short-term biological shifts translate into lasting health benefits.

Because the intervention combined three factors — probiotics, dietary counseling, and exercise — the anti-aging effects cannot be attributed to any single component. The benefit appears to come from the combination.

## The Bottom Line

The trial adds to a growing chorus of evidence that aging is not a fixed trajectory. Small, consistent lifestyle changes — many of which are already embedded in traditional Indian diets and daily routines — may genuinely slow the biological clock. The next time someone dismisses your grandmother's insistence on dahi with every meal, you might point them to the peer-reviewed literature.

*The study was published in the journal Aging and reported by the New York Post on July 10, 2026.*
